speechtext: Is the House ready for the question?

Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased to have an opportunity once again to rise and direct some comments to the new set of clauses that we are presently debating. I must say that I have some real concerns about a number of those clauses. Some of the subclauses cause concern about just what the Canadian Security Intelligence Service will mean in terms of some of the fundamental freedoms which Canadians have always thought they had.
I recall a number of such instances from my own experience. Some friends of mine had discovered that the RCMP had been conducting all sorts of investigations about some activities that presumably I had been involved in. At the time I was pursuing some scholarly endeavours and had taken it upon myself to write to a variety of countries to obtain documentation and scholarly works in order to continue my academic studies. Since this material came from foreign countries it had to arrive at Customs as its point of access. The RCMP was carrying out all sorts of investigations and interviews with some of my friends and scholarly colleagues about what

June 18, 1984
Security Intelligence Service
activities I was involved in. Obviously the RCMP felt that there was something subversive about it. But my purpose was simply to write a number of papers on a variety of foreign affairs issues.
When I discovered that there were long lists, files, reports and briefs which various agents of the RCMP had submitted about my various activities, all of which were of a scholarly and academic nature, I began to wonder about the extent to which fundamental freedoms exist in this country. Of course I was pleased, as were all Members of Parliament, when the Charter of Rights and Freedoms was introduced and passed in the House, part of which included freedom of association. I believe that all of us believe very strongly about that. People who want to work together in organizations should be allowed the freedom to do so. Yet the Bill before us makes it impossible for employees of the new service to bargain collectively. This right has been denied all of the representatives of the new intelligence service. Again, this is something embodied in the Constitution of Canada, embodied in the freedom of association clause within the Charter of Rights. To think that we are being asked now to support a clause in this Bill that goes against the very charter that all of us supported in this House of Commons seems to be bordering on the ridiculous.
That is not the worst, Mr. Speaker. When you consider that my hon. colleague from Burnaby worked so hard in committee at a time when the committee was discussing the need of the agents of the security service to swear an oath of secrecy, part of which would suggest that they would never be permitted to comment on the affairs of the service and that they would be required to carry out unlawful activities as we have all come to know them, you might say, Sir, that surely we should not be asking members of this Security Intelligence Service to carry out illegal activities.
I must say that I was shocked when I first heard from the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) that we were being asked to pass a Bill which suggested that members of the agency should be allowed to break into one's home, office or private property in search of information or intelligence material, and that it would be appropriate for agents to open first class mail at their will, having received a judicial warrant. We know how successful that is in terms of screening. Last year out of every warrant requested, virtually every single one was immediately approved. It is hardly the type of security poeple would accept as protecting their rights and freedoms. Breaking into private property, opening up first class mail, going into tax records, family allowance records and all Government documentation about an individual, having access to all private information, being able to tap telephones, and I can go on with a whole list of activities, is not in the best interests of the nation. Yet we are saying in this Bill that members of the Security Intelligence Service will be permitted to do all these things in the so-called best interests of the nation. That in itself leaves a lot to be debated.
In the clauses we are presently debating we are being asked to support the concept of individuals taking an oath of secrecy. The suggestion made by the Hon. Member for Burnaby to include lawful activities as part of this swearing in process was denied. It perplexes and concerns me that the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) would want to permit members of this agency to carry out unlawful activity under the direction of the director or other officers within the Security Intelligence Service.
When you start hearing about these various areas which cause serious concern to those involved with civil liberties in Canada, with fundamental freedoms for Canadian citizens, innocent Canadians I might add, one has to wonder, because clause after clause these shortcomings are being brought to the attention of the Solicitor General. Virtually every clause we have debated to date, and there is a whole list yet to come in the days ahead, we will be identifying the concerns we have as parliamentarians. Yet not a single one of those concerns has been answered in this House. I am hopeful that eventually we will see Members opposite rising in their places to answer some of the concerns we have. Can they explain why asking people to take an oath of secrecy that will require them to carry out unlawful activities is something we should support? I would like to hear the justification for that. I would like to hear the justification that it is appropriate now for members of the Canadian Security Intelligence Service to break and enter in pursuit of evidence, to open private mail and to get into all sorts of government confidential records. How can this be in the best interests of Canadians? How can this be in the best interests of creating an atmosphere of security in the country? This escapes me. I am hopeful and optimistic that Members opposite will shortly stand in their places and explain that we need not be concerned for these reasons. However, one does remain optimistic these days, Mr. Speaker.
In terms of the clauses we are presently debating, I must say that the points raised cause real concern, so much so that, if an adequate response is not provided, we will certainly have to vote against these clauses as they are brought forward.

Mr. Speaker, on examining the amendments that came from committee and the proposed amendments here at report stage, I regret the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) did not include one to delete Clause 4. It is there that I find what is a very definite looseness in drafting as a result of an amendment put forward in committee. But because I am precluded from making any changes, since there is no amendment at this time, all I can do is to invite Hon. Members to look at the provision to see if the term "pleasure" applies during the second term.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I would draw the attention of the Hon. Member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) to the fact that Motion No. 12 specifically refers to Clause 4 and in fact it would delete Clause 4. That will come in due course.

The point is well taken. For the information of the Hon. Members in the House, we are now

debating Motions Nos. 10, 16, 20, 25, 26, 28, and 35, which propose to delete Clauses 3, 5, 7, 9, 10, 11, and 14.

I will have to defer my point for another time, Mr. Speaker, because it concerns a clause not included in this group. I do not intend, as I have seen all too often this afternoon, to include everything but the kitchen sink in certain remarks, therefore, we will limit ourselves to particular things.
I am especially concerned about Motion No. 20 to delete Clause 7. I find it a little difficult when I see the provision stating that the director, who is to be in charge of this security service, has to consult with the Deputy Minister. What is consultation? Is it getting the consent of the Deputy Minister which regard to the operational policies of the service?
No.

Something further is added regarding any matter with respect to which consultation is required by directions issued under Clause 6(2). Here again there is something odd. Any directions issued under Clause 6(2) which are not subject to the amendment at this time, if they are later on, ought to go before the review committee. What is the review committee to do with them? Is it to be a toothless tiger as the one proposed in Bill C-24 dealing with Crown corporations? Is it to table certain things in the House and in the other place with no direction on what to do with them? Presumably they will be here for information purposes.
I would have to ask the direction of the committee as to Clause 7(2). When there is a question of applying for a warrant under Section 21 or Section 23, the director or the person so designated will consult with the Deputy Minister before applying for the warrant or the renewal of the warrant. What for? Why does the Deputy Minister have to consent to the issuance of a warrant under Section 21 or Section 23? Is the director who is running the operation not sufficient? The director is responsible to the Minister. Will he run his shop or will he run it with the Deputy Minister riding on his shoulder like an old owl? These are questions which I have to ask. Why was the amendment put in?
They were all asked at committee and answered.

I am outside the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. What is the purpose of the amendment? What sort of bureaucratic monster is being created? Is it to operate or is it not? I am looking at something which is before me. I am not looking at the present system wherein the Royal Canadian Mounted Police is operating the security agency, which is where my colleagues have decided that it should remain. I am looking at something which has been put forward now, a civilian agency. Presumably it is the result of government policy and of the government majority on the committee. Therefore, it is the entire responsibility of the Government.
Security Intelligence Service
For instance, I want to know from the Minister why the Deputy Minister, if the director is responsible to the Minister, has to be consulted with regard to special warrants. The Deputy Minister is already responsible to the Minister. Why does the director have this two-headed authority over him with regard to special warrants? Then, on top of that there is this bureaucratic excess. If there is to be a renewal, what would happen if the Deputy Minister was not around? Deputy Ministers do not sit in their offices or at home waiting for calls. Who is the designated official below the Deputy Minister? Who is to exercise authority?
If I were to be the director of this operation, I would supposedly be directly responsible to the Minister. Either I am or I am not. However, suddenly I find that the Deputy Minister will have a hand in the issuance of directions by the Minister to the director. Why? Why say that the director is responsible to the Minister? He is not. The Commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police reports through the Deputy Minister. That is the case now. That was an aberration of some years ago. That aberration is being continued by the report coming through the Deputy Minister. I think one would require a specialist to be head of the security service, but he does not get to his Minister unless he goes through the Deputy Minister. There are so many hobbles placed upon him that the Deputy Minister has control of the written instructions which are to be given to the director.
I do not know whether it is the careful hand of bureaucracy coming into play. It did before. It should never have. Running the RCMP calls for a special skill. Running the security agency will require a special skill. Why do they have to be funnelled through a Deputy Minister? The responsibility is that of the Minister who has available senior specialists. Why have the Deputy Minister? That is the question which I invite the Minister to answer?
As an individual I am looking at what the Government is now proposing. I say that there is a fundamental fallacy. I will not say that my mind is forever shut on it, but as I see it now it is a fundamental fallacy. I would like the Minister to tell me, not just because it has happened for the past 15 years, why we are continuing that tradition. I say it was a mistake 15 years ago to have the Commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police report through the Deputy Minister.

speakeroldname: Hon. Bob Kaplan (Solicitor General of Canada):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, because the Hon. Member asked such a pointed question and a good one, I ought to take just a moment to answer it. I do not want to delay opposition Members, who I know are very anxious to prolong the debate, in their opportunity to speak.
There is a very good answer to the good question which the Hon. Member asked. I receive a large number of files every day from each of the four agencies within my Ministry. Usually they recommend one course of action. I have to deal with them very quickly. Some days there could be 20 to 25

June 18, 1984
Security Intelligence Service
different ones. They come from the Commissioner of the RCMP who has the status of Deputy Minister. They come from the Commissioner of the Correctional Service of Canada who has the status of Deputy Minister. They come from the National Parole Board where there is a Deputy Minister with the status of chairman.
In each case I like to obtain an outside opinion about the advice being offered to me and the decision I am being asked to make. The outside opinion which I seek is that of my Deputy Minister. We have established in the Government of Canada over the last 14 years a secretariat made up of criminologists, sociologists and lawyers brought in from the Department of Justice and others. The secretariat has been specially set up to analyze all the documents that are being transmitted to me, all these requests for approval that are coming to me, and to give me an advice. I consider that advice to be very helpful. I do not think of it as being an extra layer of bureaucracy. I think of it as being very useful for a Minister to be able to respond promptly and get a broader picture than sometimes comes from the head of an agency. When I was designing the structure of the new security service, I wanted to be certain that that special input of secretariat-added guidance and advice would be there. That is the reason that the clause appears. With some of the other agencies that report to me, it is established by administrative directive or practice. However, I wanted the country to know about the secretariat, about the useful role it plays in giving advice to the Minister.
Consultation is just that. It does not mean that my Deputy Minister in the secretariat is suddenly responsible for running the RCMP or any other agencies. Consultation is just that. I consider it to be very valuable. I hope that the Hon. Member opposite will not vote to delete this very important clause.
